---
title: "A4 exercises — Osmotic challenges and renal accounting"
---

Use the [tutorial](index.qmd). These tasks use supplied hypothetical data and
schematics, with no sampling or fluid-manipulation procedure. Allow 60–90
minutes. Leave with a habitat comparison, a labelled nephron and an excretion
calculation that distinguishes amount from concentration.

## 1. State the membrane and the tendency

A hypothetical animal's body fluids have osmolarity 300 mOsm L⁻¹. Compare
two external media: 10 and 1,000 mOsm L⁻¹. Assuming the relevant surface
allows water exchange, predict the water tendency in each. Which additional
information would be needed to predict the flux of a particular ion?

For ideal solutions, estimate osmolarities of 0.15 mol L⁻¹ glucose and
0.15 mol L⁻¹ NaCl, treating NaCl as fully dissociated. Explain why an equal
total osmolarity does not guarantee equal tonicity for a cell membrane.

## 2. Compare freshwater and seawater teleosts

Draw one water arrow and one net salt-challenge arrow for each fish. Add
drinking behaviour, the role of gill transport and expected relative urine
volume. Explain why these examples cannot be transferred unchanged to a
marine shark or every marine invertebrate.

Your figure should distinguish a passive tendency from an active compensating
process, using different arrow labels.

## 3. Account for a substance in the kidney

For a hypothetical solute, glomerular filtration rate is 0.10 L min⁻¹ and
plasma concentration 5 mmol L⁻¹. Assume the solute is freely filtered.
Reabsorption is 0.40 mmol min⁻¹ and secretion 0.02 mmol min⁻¹.

Calculate filtered load and excretion rate. Urine flow is 0.002 L min⁻¹:
calculate urine concentration. Check that concentration × urine flow returns
the excretion rate.

Then halve urine flow while holding that excretion rate fixed. What happens
to urine concentration? Does this require the amount of solute excreted per
minute to increase?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Filtered load is filtration rate × plasma concentration. Keep L min⁻¹,
mmol L⁻¹ and mmol min⁻¹ distinct at each step.
:::

## 4. Trace water recovery and feedback

Draw a nephron route from glomerulus to collecting duct, with arrows for
filtration, reabsorption and secretion. Explain how a medullary gradient and
collecting-duct water permeability work together. Predict the direction of
change in urine volume when ADH action rises, provided the relevant gradient
and kidney function are intact.

Complete a negative-feedback explanation for an increase in body-fluid osmotic
concentration. Identify what is sensed, what responds and how the initial
disturbance is reduced. Explain why ADH does not create water.

## 5. Connect nitrogen form to trade-offs

Compare ammonia, urea and uric acid in terms of conversion costs, water demands
and physiological context. Explain why “uric acid is best because it saves
water” is incomplete. Distinguish nitrogen excretion from loss of undigested
food in faeces.

## 6. Interpret a described kidney section

An invented description reports many epithelial rings around lumens and some
capillary tufts within surrounding spaces. Propose an organ and tissue features
supporting that interpretation. Explain why one ring cannot confidently identify
a nephron segment without additional features. Connect one observed feature
to filtration and another to selective transport.

Finish with the [quiz](quiz.qmd).
